intro: Excerpts from the live EasyFlow source (C:\APPS\EasyFlow). EasyFlow has three surfaces driven by one config: the browser extension (Extension/), the Apps Script classifier (EasyFlow_AppsScript.js), and the Python dashboard + Gmail tools (Tools/app.py, create_*.py). Each snippet shows the real code behind a capability and how config.json flows into it.

sections.category: Config — the single source of truth

snippets.title: The tier configuration
snippets.explanation: This one file defines everything: six tiers, their Gmail palette colors, the nested sub-labels, and the sender/subject rules for each. The Apps Script classifier, the Gmail filters, the label tree, and the extension's rules engine are all derived from it — change a rule here and every surface re-derives. settings holds the cadence (classify every 15 min, triage stale mail after 30 days).

snippets.title: Backed-up config save
snippets.code:
def save_config(config):
    # Backup before saving
    backup_path = CONFIG_FILE + '.bak'
    if os.path.exists(CONFIG_FILE):
        import shutil
        shutil.copy2(CONFIG_FILE, backup_path)

    with open(CONFIG_FILE, 'w', encoding='utf-8') as f:
        json.dump(config, f, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False)
snippets.explanation: Because config.json is the source of truth for every surface, a bad edit could mis-sort an entire inbox. save_config() copies the current file to config.json.bak before overwriting, so the previous good configuration is always one file away. ensure_ascii=False preserves non-Latin sender names and keywords.

sections.category: Gmail API auth — Flask (OAuth + token store)

snippets.title: OAuth flow with PKCE over localhost
snippets.feature: Connect your Gmail account from the dashboard
snippets.code:
os.environ['OAUTHLIB_INSECURE_TRANSPORT'] = '1'  # allow OAuth over http://localhost

@app.route('/connect')
def connect_gmail():
    flow = Flow.from_client_secrets_file(
        find_client_secret(), scopes=GMAIL_SCOPES,
        redirect_uri='http://localhost:8550/oauth/callback')
    authorization_url, state = flow.authorization_url(
        access_type='offline', include_granted_scopes='true', prompt='consent')
    session['oauth_state'] = state
    session['code_verifier'] = flow.code_verifier   # store PKCE verifier for the callback
    return redirect(authorization_url)

@app.route('/oauth/callback')
def oauth_callback():
    flow = Flow.from_client_secrets_file(find_client_secret(), scopes=GMAIL_SCOPES,
        redirect_uri='http://localhost:8550/oauth/callback')
    flow.code_verifier = session.get('code_verifier')
    flow.fetch_token(authorization_response=request.url)
    with open(TOKEN_FILE, 'w', encoding='utf-8') as f:
        f.write(flow.credentials.to_json())
snippets.explanation: The dashboard never needs a terminal to authenticate. It runs a standard Google OAuth2 Authorization-Code-with-PKCE flow entirely in the browser: /connect redirects to Google, and /oauth/callback exchanges the code for credentials, restoring the PKCE code_verifier from the Flask session. OAUTHLIB_INSECURE_TRANSPORT lets the loopback redirect work over plain http on localhost. The token is persisted to token_gmail.json.

snippets.title: Token refresh helper
snippets.explanation: Every Gmail operation in the dashboard goes through this helper. It loads the saved credentials, silently refreshes them with the refresh token when expired (writing the new token back), and returns a (service, error) tuple so each route can surface a clean message instead of crashing. EasyFlow keeps three separate tokens by scope: token_gmail.json (labels+modify), token_gmail_filters.json (settings.basic), token_apps_script.json (script.projects).

snippets.title: Chrome getAuthToken with Edge fallback
snippets.feature: Sign-in that works in both Chrome and Edge
snippets.explanation: Chrome's chrome.identity.getAuthToken is fast but Edge doesn't implement it. getAuthToken() probes the Chrome path once; if it fails with an 'unsupported'/'Microsoft Edge' error it switches to chrome.identity.launchWebAuthFlow against a separate Web OAuth client and caches the token itself (the web flow has no built-in cache). _authMethod remembers which path worked so it never re-probes an unsupported API. This single function is what lets one codebase ship to both the Chrome and Edge stores.

snippets.title: Resilient gmailFetch (timeout + retry)
snippets.feature: Hardened Gmail REST access for bulk ops
snippets.explanation: MV3 service workers have no default fetch timeout, so a dropped Gmail response would hang forever. gmailFetch adds an AbortController hard timeout (10s for reads, 60s for destructive DELETE/batchModify), refreshes the token and retries once on 401, backs off exponentially on 429, and retries network errors twice with 2s/4s backoff. This is the foundation every label, message, and filter call in the extension is built on — it's what makes bulk cleanup and migration safe.

snippets.title: Gmail's cascade-404 is not an error
snippets.explanation: Deleting a parent label like '6 - Low Priority' makes Gmail silently delete all of its children too. Code that then tries to delete each child individually hits a 404. This helper recognises that specific case so the cleanup loop treats it as success-already-done rather than surfacing a scary error to the user.

snippets.title: The classifier core
snippets.explanation: The deterministic heart of EasyFlow. It lowercases the sender and subject, runs any special rule first (e.g. routing Rokid order mail to a different tier than Rokid news), then walks TIER_RULES in order: the first sender-domain or subject-keyword match wins and returns the full 'Tier/Sub-label' name. A null means nothing matched, so the message goes to Triage. TIER_RULES is generated verbatim from config.json.

snippets.title: The 15-minute sweep
snippets.feature: Auto-classify new mail and archive it
snippets.explanation: Registered to run every 15 minutes on Google's servers. For each unread inbox thread it classifies the latest message, applies both the sub-label and its parent tier label (so '3 - Life Admin/Bills/Internet' also gets '3 - Life Admin'), then archives the thread out of the inbox. A 5-minute runtime guard keeps it safely inside the Apps Script 6-minute execution quota. getLabel_() memoizes label lookups so each label is fetched/created once per run.

snippets.title: Trigger registration
snippets.explanation: Run once by the user after pasting/deploying the script. It clears any existing triggers (so re-running is idempotent) and registers the two time-based jobs: the 15-minute classifier and the nightly stale-inbox triage at 1 AM. After this, EasyFlow keeps sorting mail with nothing of its own running on the user's machine.

snippets.title: Generating the Apps Script from config
snippets.feature: Compile TIER_RULES from the tier tree
snippets.code:
lines.append('const TIER_RULES = {')
for tier_name, tier_data in config['tiers'].items():
    for label_name, rules in tier_data.get('labels', {}).items():
        full_label = f"{tier_name}/{label_name}"
        from_list = json.dumps(rules.get('from', []))
        subject_list = json.dumps(rules.get('subject', []))
        lines.append(f'  "{full_label}": {{')
        lines.append(f'    from: {from_list},')
        lines.append(f'    subject: {subject_list}')
        lines.append('  },')
lines.append('};')
# Append the static engine (classifyMessage_, classifyNewEmails, triage, setupTriggers)
lines.append(get_engine_code())
return '\n'.join(lines)
snippets.explanation: This is the bridge from the JSON config to runnable automation. It serializes every tier's sub-labels and rules into the TIER_RULES JS object — keyed by the full 'Tier/Sub-label' name — then appends the static engine code. The result is written to EasyFlow_AppsScript.js (POST /api/generate-script) or pushed straight to the user's Apps Script project. The generated file carries a 'do not edit directly' header pointing back to the dashboard.

snippets.title: Compiling tier rules into Gmail filters
snippets.explanation: The alternative to the Apps Script: native Gmail filters that need zero software running. Each tier rule becomes one or more filter definitions, with senders and subject keywords batched five-per-query (Gmail filter queries get unwieldy beyond that). When created (via /api/filters/create), each filter adds its tier label and removes INBOX — so matching mail is auto-filed and skips the inbox the moment it arrives.

snippets.title: Pushing the script via the Apps Script API
snippets.code:
service = build('script', 'v1', credentials=creds)
request_body = {'files': [
    {'name': 'Code', 'type': 'SERVER_JS', 'source': script_code},
    {'name': 'appsscript', 'type': 'JSON', 'source': json.dumps({
        "timeZone": "America/New_York",
        "oauthScopes": [
            "https://www.googleapis.com/auth/gmail.modify",
            "https://www.googleapis.com/auth/gmail.labels",
            "https://www.googleapis.com/auth/script.scriptapp"],
        "runtimeVersion": "V8"})}]}
service.projects().updateContent(scriptId=script_id, body=request_body).execute()
snippets.explanation: Instead of copy-pasting the generated code into the Apps Script editor, the dashboard can push it directly with the Apps Script API. projects().updateContent() replaces the project's files with the freshly generated classifier plus an appsscript manifest declaring the V8 runtime and Gmail scopes. This needs a saved script ID and the script.projects token (token_apps_script.json); 403/404 errors are translated into plain-language guidance. Status: partial — manual copy-paste remains the fallback.

snippets.title: AI triage batch with tier guard
snippets.explanation: When the deterministic rules can't place an email, the AI is asked. A pre-flight guard refuses to run with no tiers (the model would have no targets). It builds validTargets from the actual tier tree, sends only the From/Subject/snippet — never the body — to the chosen LLM, and crucially only accepts a suggestion if the returned label already exists in the user's tree. That guard is what stops the model inventing categories. Capped at 200 messages per run.

snippets.title: The Gemini provider adapter
snippets.explanation: One of four interchangeable provider adapters (Gemini, Ollama, OpenAI-compatible, Anthropic). The key comes from the user's own settings in chrome.storage.local — EasyFlow pays nothing per email. The locale-aware system prompt makes the assistant answer in the user's chosen language. callProvider() picks the right adapter for chat; callLLMForClassification() picks it for triage. Only metadata and snippets ever leave the browser.

snippets.title: Auth-gated entry + dashboard stats
snippets.explanation: The dashboard is a desktop convenience, not a server — it binds to 127.0.0.1:8550 (within EasyFlow's 8550-8559 registry block) and auto-opens the browser on launch. The root route gates on Gmail authentication, sending first-time users to the welcome wizard and everyone else to the dashboard, where get_stats() summarises the config (total labels, senders, subjects, rules) into the overview cards.

snippets.title: Tier CRUD with proper status codes
snippets.feature: Edit the tier tree via the designer
snippets.explanation: The designer and configure pages call a small REST API to mutate the tier tree: POST adds a sub-label, PUT updates its rules, DELETE removes it, and /api/designer/save replaces the whole tree at once. Each handler returns honest HTTP status codes — 400 for missing input, 404 for an unknown tier, 409 for a duplicate label — and every successful mutation runs through the backed-up save_config().

snippets.title: Promise-wrapped messaging
snippets.explanation: The side panel is a thin UI; all Gmail work happens in the service worker. sendMessage() wraps the callback-style chrome.runtime.sendMessage in a Promise so the panel can `await` worker actions. resolveWildcardLabels() is a good example: typing a pattern like '2*' sends a resolveWildcard request and the worker returns every matching label name, so one command can operate on a whole group of labels.

snippets.title: Stuck-label retry state machine
snippets.explanation: Gmail occasionally fails to delete a label under load. Rather than retry forever, EasyFlow uses a bounded state machine: attempt 1 retries the failed label IDs, attempt 2 retries once more, and if labels are still stuck after that it stops and shows the user explicit manual-cleanup instructions (guideManualCleanup) instead of spinning. This keeps the UI honest about what it could and couldn't do.
